title: a non-numeric `in_degree` is rejected in both languages via TWO DIFFERENT failure paths that share one leading clause
error_substring: in_degree must be a positive integer
why: Fixture content is row01's golden with `in_degree`'s value replaced by the
string 'not_a_number' (AMENDED from an earlier draft's literal `in_degree: 0`,
since a literal zero exercises NEITHER
promised path — C++'s `strtoll` parses `0` legitimately, and Python's
`isinstance(value, int)` accepts a real `0` — so it pinned nothing).
This ONE row exercises BOTH promised failure paths: C++'s
integer scanner is type-blind by construction — `strtoll` of a
non-numeric JSON string collapses to 0, and the positive-integer check
then rejects it with '... got 0'; Python's field is read as a real JSON
string, so its `isinstance(value, int)` type check rejects it directly
with '... got 'not_a_number''. The two languages therefore fail via
DIFFERENT internal mechanisms and DIFFERENT trailing text, which is
exactly why the asserted substring stops BEFORE the divergent `got` tail
language-invariant LEADING clause; what follows is presentation).
`host_add_plugin` is exercised too: its only structural gate is the
shared validator, so both failure paths are reachable through it as well.
